content.title: About
content.content: Taro (Colocasia esculenta) is a large tropical perennial plant cultivated for its starchy corms. After cooking, the corms become soft, slightly sweet, and creamy in texture. Taro is used in soups, purees, casseroles, and as a side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Taro has been cultivated for more than 10,000 years, making it one of the world’s oldest staple crops.
In some cultures the leaves are eaten as a vegetable, while in others they are used for weaving mats and paper.
Raw taro contains oxalates and calcium‑oxalate crystals that can irritate skin and mucous membranes.
Taro is sometimes called “earth apple” because of its mildly sweet, potato‑like flavor.
In Hawaii, the traditional dish “poi” made from mashed cooked taro is a cultural emblem.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Taro provides both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion and blood‑sugar regulation.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C in taro helps boost immunity and participates in collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium aids in fluid balance and normal heart function.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Taro supplies vitamin B6 and folate, important for metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: With virtually no fat, taro is suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Raw toxicity
items.content: Uncooked corms contain oxalates and calcium‑oxalate crystals that can cause stomach irritation and kidney issues; they must be fully cooked before eating.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic responses such as skin itching or swelling.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Taro has a high GI, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Boil taro corms until tender (about 20‑30 minutes), then use them in purees, soups, casseroles, or as a side dish. Butter, milk, or spices can be added for flavor. Do not eat raw corms.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked taro in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Raw corms keep in a cool, dry place for up to 2 weeks but should be cooked as soon as possible.
